lead: Ocean routes follow the planet's wind belts. One thing you avoid at any price: the tropical revolving storm, where your hemisphere decides every action.

sections.title: Trades, doldrums and westerlies

qa.q: Which way do the trade winds blow in each hemisphere?
qa.a: NE in the northern hemisphere, SE in the southern: the **trades** flow from the highs near 30° back towards the ITCZ, the doldrums, turned by Coriolis.

refs: The ITCZ — Panama to the Galápagos
El Niño — cyclones and the trades

blocks.p: Air rises at the **ITCZ**, the doldrums: calms and squalls. It sinks near 30° in a belt of highs, the **horse latitudes**, and flows back as the **trades**, turned by Coriolis: NE in the northern hemisphere, SE in the southern. Poleward blow the **westerlies** with their lows, then the polar easterlies.

fig.note: Schematic · the belts shift north and south with the Sun

blocks.p: The ITCZ follows the Sun and is wider in the east: cross it further west, with fuel for the calms. Winter highs reinforce the trades to 25–30 kn; El Niño weakens the Pacific trades and moves the cyclones east. Trade-wind **squalls** travel with the wind and can double it: reef before they arrive.

sections.title: Which side of the high to sail

qa.q: Which side of an ocean high should I sail to avoid the calms?
qa.a: Keep out of its calm centre: the **trades** blow on a high's equatorward side, the westerlies on its poleward side. Wind circles it clockwise in the northern hemisphere, anticlockwise in the southern; route by where it lies today.

refs: Subtropical highs — the North Pacific High
Subtropical highs — the St Helena High
Subtropical highs — the Azores High's movement

blocks.p: Wind circles a high clockwise in the northern hemisphere, anticlockwise in the southern. Either way the trades blow on its equatorward side, the westerlies on its poleward side, calms in the centre. Route by where it lies today.

A **monsoon** reverses with the season: in the northern Indian Ocean and the South China Sea the NE monsoon (November–March) is fair, the SW monsoon (June–September) blows force 6–7, and between them come calms, squalls and cyclones. The Red Sea is NNW all year, except SSE in its southern half in winter.

sections.title: Let the low pass on the poleward side

qa.q: Which side should I let a depression pass when sailing east across an ocean?
qa.a: On your **poleward side**: lows travel east, and with the centre passing poleward of you the wind stays westerly and fair, veering SW to NW in the northern hemisphere, backing NW to SW in the southern.

refs: Depressions — fronts on an ocean crossing
Southern Ocean — lows and their sequence

blocks.p: Lows travel east, turning anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere and clockwise in the southern. Bound east, let the centre pass on your poleward side: the wind stays westerly and fair.
The cold front brings the shift, squalls and a rising glass. Southern Ocean lows come in a train: a brief ridge, then NW wind and a falling glass for the next.

sections.title: Where and when, and the first signs

qa.q: What are the first warning signs of a hurricane or tropical cyclone at sea?
qa.a: A long swell from the storm's bearing, cirrus fanning from one point, then the barometer: corrected for its daily 3 hPa swing, 3 hPa below normal means suspect a **tropical revolving storm**, 5 means act.

refs: Tropical revolving storms — where they form

blocks.p: A **tropical revolving storm** needs a sea of 26.5 °C and Coriolis, so it forms at least 5° from the equator, in its hemisphere's summer and autumn. It moves west and poleward, then **recurves** towards the pole and east, faster.

fig.note: Northern hemisphere: dangerous half right of the track
Southern hemisphere: dangerous half left of the track

blocks.p: First signs: a long swell from the storm's bearing, cirrus fanning from one point, then the barometer. Tropical pressure swings 3 hPa daily (high 1000 and 2200, low 0400 and 1600); corrected for that, 3 hPa below normal means suspect, 5 means act. In the **eye** the wind drops, then returns as hard from the opposite side.

sections.title: Find the centre, then act by hemisphere

qa.q: Which way should I steer to get clear of a tropical revolving storm?
qa.a: Keep the wind on the starboard bow, close-hauled, if it veers and you are in the **dangerous semicircle**; on the starboard quarter, running, if it backs or holds steady with a falling glass. South of the equator it is port, and backing means dangerous.

refs: Tropical revolving storms — Buys Ballot's law
Tropical revolving storms — the centre's bearing
Tropical revolving storms — finding the centre
Tropical revolving storms — a stalled storm
Tropical revolving storms — a catamaran's options

blocks.p: **Buys Ballot's law**: face the wind and the centre is about 10 points (112°) to your right in the northern hemisphere, to your left in the southern.

In the **dangerous semicircle** the storm's speed adds to the wind, and the wind carries you into its path: right of the track in the northern hemisphere, left in the southern. The other half is **navigable**. The wind shift tells you which half you are in; so does the centre's bearing: moving clockwise, you are right of the track.

blocks.rule: North: wind to starboard. South: wind to port. Bow in the dangerous half, quarter in the navigable.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **1-2-3 rule** adds 100, 200 and 300 M to the 34-knot radius at 24, 48 and 72 hours: forecast error grows. The gale arrives at (distance − radius) ÷ speed. Move early; a stalled storm can go anywhere.

sections.title: What the wind does to moving water

qa.q: Why should I not cross the Gulf Stream with a northerly wind?
qa.a: **Wind against current** raises short, steep, breaking seas, and the Gulf Stream sets NE at 3 kn: cross it, or ride the Agulhas, only with the wind going its way.

blocks.p: Wind against current raises short, steep, breaking seas: cross the Gulf Stream or ride the Agulhas only with the wind going its way. Moist air chilled over a cold current gives **advection fog** that wind does not clear. **Swell** outruns a distant storm at 1.5 × its period, in knots. Steer across a waterspout's track.

sections.title: Climate for the plan, forecasts for the day

qa.q: Can I trust a GRIB forecast when a tropical storm is near?
qa.a: No: trust the advisory, not the **GRIB**. A GRIB shows the mean wind: gusts run 40 % higher, squalls are missing and storms blunted. Where models disagree, plan for the worse.

refs: Weather information — GRIB and its limits

blocks.p: A **pilot chart** shows one month's averages: wind roses, gale and calm percentages, ice limits, past storm tracks. It is history: an empty route means rare, not impossible.
